Iran International

The dollar traded at a record 2,802,000 rials, up around 6% from 2,642,000 on November 12. The euro climbed to 3,056,500 rials, while the British pound reached 3,653,400 rials.

The latest plunge in Iran’s currency came a day after Washington imposed sanctions on 22 entities and eight individuals involved in the Islamic Republic’s overseas financial networks.

“Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.”

The measures targeted the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which facilitates tens of billions of dollars in annual trade by connecting exporters earning foreign currency with importers.

A separate Treasury report identified $14.7 billion in transactions potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking networks between January 2025 and August 2026.

Accelerating currency depreciation

The dollar now trades at more than 3.4 times its value in June 2025, when it stood at around 820,000 rials following the outbreak of the 12-day war.

The depreciation has coincided with Washington’s tightening naval blockade and efforts to restrict Iranian oil sales and disrupt the transfer of export revenues.

100%Bundles of Iranian rial and US dollar banknotes lie on the counter of a currency exchange shop.$RS("S:d","P:d")Several economists have warned in recent months of the risk of hyperinflation as Iran grapples with declining production, foreign currency shortages and mounting trade restrictions.

Iranian officials have meanwhile blamed currency market participants for exchange rate instability.

The weakening currency is driving up the cost of imported raw materials, medicines, medical equipment and consumer goods.

For Iranian households already struggling with stagnant or overdue wages and rising housing, food and healthcare costs, the dollar’s continued rise threatens to further erode purchasing power.
